reader_situation: Someone whose kitchen junk drawer has been cleaned out before and filled back up, and who wants a version that stays organized, including what to do with the batteries, lighters, and odd items that end up there.
direct_answer: Empty it, give the drawer one job with a written list of what belongs, sort the survivors by task into bins, and check it against the list on a fixed weekly cue. Take loose and spent batteries out of the jumble: EPA says to tape terminals or bag batteries separately because lithium cells can spark if the terminals touch, and button batteries need to be kept away from young children.
consensus: Empty the drawer completely and wipe it out.
Toss, relocate, and keep only what belongs.
Use drawer dividers or modular bins.
gaps: Batteries are the junk drawer's real hazard. EPA: a lithium battery may spark and cause fires if damaged or if the terminal ends touch; tape terminals and/or put batteries in separate plastic bags; cover coin and button cell terminals with non-conductive tape such as electrical tape and keep them away from young children.

Alkaline batteries are different: EPA says most communities allow alkaline and zinc-carbon batteries in household trash, though it recommends recyclers; lithium-ion should never go in the trash (USFA, registry).

Spare lithium-ion batteries should be stored away from anything that can burn, at room temperature when possible; stop using any that show odor, color change, heat, swelling, leaking, or odd noises (USFA).

Button batteries: more than 3,500 people in the US swallow them each year; one stuck in the esophagus can cause severe damage in just 2 hours. National Battery Ingestion Hotline 1-800-498-8666; Poison Control 1-800-222-1222 (Poison Control).

The weekly check sticks better tied to a fixed cue: habit research (BJGP 2012) shows repetition in a consistent context makes an action automatic, and it must be a doing behavior ('after I..., I...').
Harvard Health recommends designating a place for items you use often, which is what a keep-list formalizes.

evidence.claim: How to store used batteries; lithium fire risk; alkaline disposal
evidence.detail: Tape battery terminals and/or place batteries in separate plastic bags. For button-cell and coin batteries, use separate bags or non-conductive tape such as electrical tape over the terminals, and keep them away from young children. A lithium battery may spark and cause fires if damaged or the terminal ends touch. In most communities, alkaline and zinc carbon batteries can be safely put in household trash; EPA recommends battery recyclers or checking with local solid waste authorities. Find recycling via Earth911 or Call2Recycle.

Store spare lithium-ion batteries away from anything that can burn. Store them at room temperature when possible; don't keep them in direct sunlight or hot cars. Stop using lithium-ion batteries if you notice an odor, change in color, too much heat, change in shape, leaking or odd noises. Don't put lithium-ion batteries in the trash.
evidence.source_title: Battery Fire Safety | U.S. Fire Administration

evidence.claim: Button battery ingestion speed and hotline
evidence.detail: Batteries stuck in the esophagus must be removed as quickly as possible as severe damage can occur in just 2 hours. National Battery Ingestion Hotline 1-800-498-8666 (24 hours), or Poison Control 1-800-222-1222. Do not induce vomiting. More than 3,500 people in the US swallow button batteries each year. Found in hearing aids, watches, toys, games, flashing jewelry, singing greeting cards, and remote controls.
evidence.source_title: Button Battery Ingestion | Poison Control (National Capital Poison Center)

evidence.claim: Designate a place for everyday items
evidence.detail: Designate a place at home for your glasses, purse, keys, and other items you use often. Remove clutter to cut down on distractions.
evidence.source_title: 7 ways to keep your memory sharp at any age (Harvard Health Publishing)

evidence.claim: Habits form by repeating an action after a consistent cue
evidence.detail: Mere repetition of a simple action in a consistent context leads, through associative learning, to the action being activated by those cues. Plan when and where; choose a time and place you encounter regularly; it is not possible to form a habit for not doing something, so choose a new behaviour to do.
evidence.source_title: Making health habitual: the psychology of 'habit-formation' and general practice (British Journal of General Practice, 2012)

evidence.claim: Absentmindedness: items set down without attention aren't remembered
evidence.detail: This type of forgetting occurs when you don't pay close enough attention; you didn't focus on where you put it in the first place, so your brain didn't encode the information securely.
evidence.source_title: Forgetfulness: 7 types of normal memory problems (Harvard Health Publishing)
